transcript.heading: News Report One (British Female)
paras: A new study has found that eating a handful of nuts every day can significantly reduce the risk of heart disease and improve overall cardiovascular health, according to researchers at Imperial College London. The study analyzed data from over 800,000 people across 20 different countries and found that people who ate at least 20 grams of nuts per day had a 30 percent lower risk of coronary heart disease and a 20 percent lower risk of stroke compared to people who rarely or never ate nuts. Researchers say nuts are rich in healthy fats, fiber, vitamins, and minerals like magnesium and potassium, which are good for heart health. They also contain antioxidants that help reduce inflammation in the body. The benefits were seen across all types of nuts, including almonds, walnuts, peanuts, and cashews, though walnuts and tree nuts showed slightly stronger effects. Researchers caution that nuts are high in calories, so people shouldn't eat too many—about a handful a day is the right amount. They also say it's important to eat plain, unsalted nuts rather than nuts coated in sugar, salt, or chocolate, which can cancel out the health benefits.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Male)
paras: The city of Barcelona in Spain has launched an ambitious plan to create "superblocks" throughout the city, turning car-filled streets into pedestrian-friendly spaces with parks, playgrounds, and community areas. A superblock is a group of nine city blocks where through traffic is restricted, and cars can only enter to access parking garages or drop off passengers, driving at very low speeds. This frees up most of the street space for pedestrians, cyclists, and community use. The plan aims to reduce traffic, air pollution, and noise, and to make the city more livable and healthier for residents. The first superblocks were introduced several years ago and have been successful, so the city is now expanding the program to cover more neighborhoods. Supporters say the superblocks have already reduced air pollution by up to 40 percent in some areas, increased foot traffic for local businesses, and created much-needed green space in the dense city. However, some residents and business owners are concerned about reduced parking access and traffic being pushed into surrounding neighborhoods. The city says it's working to address these concerns and that the long-term benefits for public health and quality of life are worth the short-term adjustments.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: Astronomers have discovered a new exoplanet— a planet outside our solar system— that is one of the most Earth-like worlds ever found, orbiting a star in the habitable zone where liquid water could exist on the surface. The planet, named TOI-700 d, is about 100 light-years from Earth and is only slightly larger than our planet. It orbits a small, cool red dwarf star, and it's located in the star's "habitable zone"— the region around a star where temperatures are just right for liquid water to exist, which is considered essential for life as we know it. Scientists say the planet receives about the same amount of energy from its star as Earth receives from the sun. While the discovery is exciting, scientists caution that we don't yet know if the planet actually has water, an atmosphere, or if it could support life. More observations will be needed with more powerful telescopes to learn more about the planet's atmosphere and composition. The discovery is still important because it shows that Earth-sized planets in habitable zones are relatively common, increasing the chances that we might one day find evidence of life beyond Earth.

7. Why is the "habitable zone" important?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Tom): Hey Sarah, I heard you're going skiing this weekend. I'm so jealous! I've always wanted to try skiing, but I've never been.
Woman (Sarah): Oh, you should definitely try it! It's so much fun. You should come with us sometime.
Man: Really? I'd love to, but I'm kind of nervous. I don't know anything about skiing. Isn't it dangerous?
Woman: It can be if you're reckless, but if you take lessons and start slow, it's pretty safe. Everyone falls a lot when they're first learning—it's part of the process.
Man: Yeah, I'm pretty clumsy. I'd probably break something.

Woman: Oh, come on, it's not that bad! You just have to start on the easy slopes—they're called bunny hills—and take it slow. And you wear a helmet and all kinds of protective gear, so it's pretty hard to seriously hurt yourself as long as you're not doing stupid stuff.
Man: Hmm, okay. But isn't it expensive? I feel like skiing is a rich person's sport.

Woman: It can be expensive, yeah. Lift tickets, equipment rental, lessons... it adds up. But there are ways to make it cheaper. If you go during the week instead of on weekends, tickets are cheaper. And you can rent equipment instead of buying it, especially when you're just starting out. A lot of places also have discounted beginner packages that include rentals and a lesson.
Man: That's good to know. What kind of gear do I need?

Woman: Well, the basics are skis, boots, and poles, which you can rent. Then you need warm, waterproof clothes—like a ski jacket and pants, thermal layers underneath, gloves or mittens, a hat or helmet liner, and goggles. Oh, and definitely a helmet. I never ski without one.
Man: That sounds like a lot of stuff.

Woman: It is, but most of it you can rent or borrow when you're first starting out. You don't need to buy everything right away. The most important thing is to dress warm and stay dry. If you get cold and wet, you'll be miserable.
Man: What about the actual skiing? Is it hard to learn?

Woman: The basics are pretty easy to pick up. You'll probably spend your first lesson just learning how to stop and turn on the bunny hill. It feels awkward at first, but it clicks pretty quickly. After a couple of lessons, you'll be able to go down the easy green runs by yourself.
Man: Green runs?

Woman: Oh right, ski runs are rated by difficulty. Green is the easiest, then blue is intermediate, black diamond is advanced, and double black diamond is expert. So you start on green and work your way up.
Man: That makes sense. How long do you think it would take me to get good enough to have fun?

Woman: Honestly, you can have fun on your first day, even if you're just going down the bunny hill and falling a lot. It's fun just being out in the mountains and trying something new. But if you want to be able to go down blue runs comfortably, that usually takes a few days of practice.
Man: Hmm, you're making me want to try it. When are you going again?
Woman: We're going next month for a long weekend. You should come! We can help you get set up with rentals and lessons, and we'll stick with you on the easy runs.
Man: That sounds awesome! Let me think about it and check if I can get the time off work.
Woman: Definitely think about it! I promise you'll have a great time. And if you hate it, you can just hang out in the lodge and drink hot chocolate. There's no pressure.
Man: Ha, that's true. Hot chocolate is always good. Alright, I'll seriously consider it.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Hannah): Hey Oliver, how's your study abroad application going? I thought the deadline was coming up soon.
Man (Oliver): Ugh, don't remind me. It's due next week and I'm so behind. I can't decide which program to apply to. There are so many options and they all sound good in different ways.
Woman: Where are you thinking of going? I remember you said you wanted to go to Europe.
Man: Yeah, I want to go somewhere in Europe, but I can't decide between Italy, Spain, and France. All three sound amazing for different reasons.
Woman: Oh, those are all great choices. What's making it so hard to decide?
Man: Well, Italy has amazing food and history, and I've always wanted to see Rome and Florence. But I don't speak any Italian, and most of the classes there are in Italian, right?

Woman: Not necessarily— a lot of study abroad programs offer classes in English, especially for international students. But it would be harder to get around and meet locals if you don't speak the language.

Man: Yeah, that's what I'm worried about. What about Spain? I took Spanish in high school, so I remember some of it. I could probably get by. And Spain has great weather, right? And the architecture is supposed to be incredible.

Woman: Spain is awesome. I studied in Barcelona for a semester and I loved it. The people are really friendly, the food is great, and there's so much to see and do. And if you already know some Spanish, that's a big advantage.

Man: That's good to hear. But then there's France. I've always wanted to go to Paris, and French culture has always fascinated me. But I don't speak any French at all, which would be even worse than Italy.
Woman: Yeah, Paris is amazing, but the language barrier would be real. And Parisians have a reputation for being... let's say, not super patient with people who don't speak French.
Man: That's what I've heard. Hmm. What about cost? Are some of these countries more expensive than others?

Woman: Definitely. France and Italy are pretty expensive, especially the big cities like Paris and Rome. Spain is a bit cheaper, especially if you go to a smaller city instead of Barcelona or Madrid. Eastern Europe is even cheaper, but I don't think you're considering that.
Man: No, I think I want to go to Western Europe. What about academics? I need to make sure the classes I take will transfer back and count toward my degree.

Woman: That's super important. You should talk to your academic advisor about which programs have classes that will transfer. There's no point in going if you can't get credit for the classes you take.
Man: Yeah, I need to do that. I've been so focused on where I want to go that I haven't really thought about the academic side enough.

Woman: Also, think about what you want to get out of the experience. Do you want to focus on learning a language? Do you want to travel a lot on weekends? Do you care more about nightlife or museums and culture? Different places are good for different things.
Man: That's a good point. I want to travel as much as possible, so maybe being in a central location would be good. Spain is pretty central, right? Easy to get to other countries from there?
Woman: Yeah, from Spain you can easily get to France, Portugal, Italy... it's a good base. And budget airlines in Europe are really cheap if you book early.
Man: Hmm, you're making Spain sound like the best option. But I'm still not sure. What would you do if you were me?

Woman: Honestly, I think you should go with Spain. You already know some Spanish, it's a bit cheaper, the weather is great, and it's a good base for traveling. But it's your decision—you should go wherever you feel most excited about.
Man: Yeah, you're right. I need to just make a decision and stop overthinking it. Thanks, Hannah. You've been really helpful.
Woman: No problem! Let me know what you decide. And if you do go to Spain, I can give you all my tips and recommendations.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The history of the internet is a story of rapid innovation and global connection that has transformed almost every aspect of modern life. What started as a small military research project has grown into a global network that connects billions of people around the world.

The origins of the internet go back to the 1960s, when the United States Department of Defense started a research project called ARPANET. The goal was to create a decentralized communications network that could survive a nuclear attack by routing messages through multiple paths. The first message was sent over ARPANET in 1969 between computers at UCLA and Stanford, and the network grew from there, connecting more and more universities and research institutions.

In the 1970s and 1980s, the network continued to grow, and important technologies like TCP/IP—the set of rules that govern how data is sent over the internet—were developed. The term "internet" was first used in 1983, when ARPANET switched to using TCP/IP protocols.

The internet as we know it today really started to take shape in the early 1990s, when a British computer scientist named Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web while working at CERN in Switzerland. Before the web, the internet was mostly text-based and used mainly by researchers and academics. The web made it possible to have websites with images, links, and multimedia content, and it made the internet much easier to use for ordinary people.

The first web browser was released in 1993, and the internet quickly grew in popularity. By the mid-1990s, millions of people were using the internet, and companies were starting to see its commercial potential. The dot-com boom of the late 1990s saw thousands of internet startups launch, though many of them failed when the bubble burst in 2000.

The 2000s and 2010s saw the rise of social media, smartphones, and mobile internet, which made the internet even more accessible and integrated into daily life. Today, over 4 billion people—more than half the world's population—use the internet, and it has transformed how we communicate, work, learn, shop, and entertain ourselves.

The internet has brought enormous benefits, but it has also created new challenges, like misinformation, privacy concerns, cybercrime, and issues with digital addiction. As the internet continues to evolve, societies will have to figure out how to maximize its benefits while minimizing its harms.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Music has been part of human culture for thousands of years, and it exists in every society on Earth. But why do humans make music? And what effect does it have on our brains and bodies? Recent research in neuroscience has shown that music has profound effects on the brain, affecting everything from our emotions to our memory to our physical health.

One of the most well-known effects of music is its ability to influence our mood. Upbeat, fast music can make us feel energized and happy, while slow, calm music can help us relax and reduce stress. This isn't just psychological—music actually causes physical changes in the body. Listening to music you enjoy releases dopamine in the brain, the same chemical that's released when you eat good food or do other pleasurable activities. It can also lower cortisol, the stress hormone, and reduce heart rate and blood pressure.

Music also has powerful effects on memory. That's why a song from your past can bring back vivid memories and emotions, even from many years ago. Music activates many different areas of the brain at once, including areas involved in memory, emotion, and movement. This is why music therapy can be effective for people with memory loss and dementia—familiar music can often reach parts of the brain that other forms of communication can't.

Interestingly, playing music has even stronger effects on the brain than just listening to it. Learning to play an instrument is like a full-body workout for the brain, engaging visual, auditory, and motor cortices all at once. Studies have shown that children who learn to play music have better academic performance, improved memory, and better spatial reasoning skills. And for adults, playing music can help keep the brain sharp as we age.

Music also has social functions. Making music together—singing in a choir, playing in a band, even just dancing together—releases oxytocin, the "bonding hormone," and strengthens social connections. This might be one reason why music has been so important in human cultures throughout history—it helps build community and social cohesion.

Scientists are still learning about all the ways music affects us, but one thing is clear: music is much more than just entertainment. It's a fundamental part of what makes us human, with powerful effects on our brains, our bodies, and our relationships with each other.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: The global water crisis is one of the most pressing challenges of the 21st century. While water covers about 70 percent of the Earth's surface, only about 2.5 percent of that is fresh water, and much of that is locked up in glaciers and ice caps. As the world's population grows and climate change worsens, access to clean, safe drinking water is becoming increasingly difficult for billions of people around the world.

Today, about 2 billion people don't have access to safely managed drinking water, and nearly twice that many don't have access to proper sanitation. Water scarcity affects every continent, and it's getting worse as populations grow, urbanization increases, and climate change alters rainfall patterns and causes more frequent droughts.

There are many causes of the global water crisis. One major cause is simply overuse—people are using water faster than it can be replenished. Agriculture is the biggest user of water, accounting for about 70 percent of global freshwater use, much of it wasted through inefficient irrigation methods. Industry and domestic use also consume large amounts of water.

Pollution is another major cause. Industrial waste, agricultural runoff, and untreated sewage pollute rivers, lakes, and groundwater, making water unsafe to drink and damaging aquatic ecosystems. In many developing countries, most wastewater is released back into the environment without being treated.

Climate change is making the water crisis worse. Rising temperatures increase evaporation and cause more droughts in some regions, while changing weather patterns cause more intense floods in others. Melting glaciers, which are an important source of fresh water for billions of people, are shrinking due to global warming.

The consequences of the water crisis are severe. Lack of access to clean water and sanitation causes millions of deaths every year from waterborne diseases like cholera and diarrhea. Water scarcity also leads to food shortages, because you can't grow food without water. It can cause conflicts over limited water resources, and it can lead to mass migration as people leave areas that have become uninhabitable.

But there are solutions. Improving water efficiency, especially in agriculture, can save huge amounts of water. Treating and reusing wastewater can provide a reliable source of water for irrigation and other uses. Protecting watersheds and wetlands can help maintain clean water supplies. And new technologies like desalination—turning salt water into fresh water—are becoming more affordable, though they still have environmental costs.

Addressing the global water crisis will require cooperation between governments, businesses, and individuals. It's one of the defining challenges of our time, but it's not impossible to solve. With the right policies, technologies, and investments, we can ensure that everyone has access to clean, safe water.
